debt.say: Alright, this is Module 2, Debt, and we start with the language of bonds. A bond is a loan to a government, municipality or company: the issuer pays coupons and returns principal at maturity, under a contract called the indenture. Two exam defaults to lock in: par is one thousand dollars, and coupons are paid semiannually. A basis point is one hundredth of one percent. Below par is a discount, above par a premium, and a bond issued below par carries original issue discount. Maturity buckets: under a year is money market, one to five is short, five to ten intermediate, over ten long, and longer means more price volatility. Walk the example: a thousand-dollar bond with a three and a half percent coupon pays thirty-five dollars a year, which is seventeen fifty every six months, not thirty-five. If its yield moves from four point two oh to four point nine five percent, that's seventy-five basis points, not seven and a half. And with the yield above the coupon, it trades at a discount. On ratings, an upgrade means yield falls and price rises; a downgrade, the reverse. High-yield bonds track the issuer's business, so they correlate more with stocks and are poor diversifiers for an all-stock portfolio. The exam trap: the investment-grade line is triple-B minus at S&P, Baa at Moody's. Double-B plus sounds close, but it's junk. To a client: the rating is a grade on how likely the issuer is to pay you back, and below triple-B you're paid more because the odds of a missed payment are higher.

Now the risks. Start with the idea: a bond's value is the present value of its coupons plus the present value of its principal, so anything that changes the discount rate or threatens those cash flows is a risk. Interest rate risk is the core: rates rise, price falls. Reinvestment rate risk is the flip side: rates fall, your coupons and principal get reinvested lower, and realized return comes in under the yield to maturity. Here's the clean split: interest rate risk hits today's price; reinvestment risk hits what the cash earns next. A zero-coupon bond has the highest interest rate risk but, as an exam rule, no reinvestment risk. Call risk means the issuer redeems after rates fall, capping the price near the call price. Default risk is the issuer failing to pay. Purchasing power risk is inflation eroding fixed payments. And exchange rate risk, so walk the example. A U.S. investor buys a ten-thousand-euro bond when one euro equals a dollar ten, so it costs eleven thousand dollars. At maturity the euro is worth a dollar oh four, so the proceeds are ten thousand four hundred: a six-hundred-dollar loss even though the bond paid in full. A stronger dollar shrinks foreign-currency proceeds. The exam trap: Treasuries are default-risk free, not risk free. They still carry interest rate, reinvestment and purchasing power risk. To a client: a bond can lose value even if the issuer never misses a payment, because if rates go up, newer bonds pay more and yours is worth less if you sell before maturity.

Treasuries are default-risk free, and the interest is federally taxed but exempt from state and local tax. STRIPS take each coupon and the principal of a note or bond and sell them as separate zeros. They're deep discount, very rate-sensitive, have no call risk, and you buy them through brokers or dealers, not the Treasury. The accrued interest is taxed every year, so they're best in tax-deferred accounts. TIPS index the principal to CPI, and each payment is the adjusted principal times the coupon divided by two. Walk both examples. Strip a twenty-thousand-dollar, five-year, three percent note: ten semiannual coupons of three hundred dollars plus one twenty-thousand-dollar principal piece, eleven separate zeros. Now twenty thousand of a one point eight percent TIPS, with CPI up two percent in six months. Principal becomes twenty thousand four hundred, and the payment is that times point nine percent, one hundred eighty-three sixty. That four-hundred-dollar step-up is federal ordinary income that year, and because it was taxed, it's added to basis. Savings bonds: EE bonds earn a fixed rate for life; I bonds combine a fixed rate with a semiannual CPI-based rate. Hold at least twelve months, and redeeming within five years costs three months of interest. The interest can be excluded for qualified higher education, subject to an AGI phaseout. The trap: TIPS keep a fixed rate, and the dollar payment changes because the principal changes. And STRIPS can't be bought from the Treasury. To a client: TIPS grow your principal with inflation, but the IRS taxes that growth every year, so we'd rather hold them in your IRA.

Agencies and mortgage pass-throughs, where the backing matters most. GNMA, Ginnie Mae, carries a direct U.S. guarantee; it buys FHA and VA mortgages and guarantees timely principal and interest on its pass-throughs. The Farm Credit Administration is also direct. Freddie Mac, Fannie Mae and Sallie Mae are indirect, so they pay slightly higher coupons. Fannie and Freddie have been in FHFA conservatorship since 2008, and the textbook says Treasury's support amounts to an explicit guarantee. Tax note: unlike Treasuries, agency interest is generally taxable federally and by states. Now pass-throughs. Monthly mortgage interest and principal, less servicing, flow to investors, so every check includes a return of your own capital. That's what trips retirees up. Walk it: a retiree holds eighty thousand of pass-throughs and spends every check. Over a year, six thousand dollars of those checks was principal, so the invested base is now about seventy-four thousand, and next year's interest is earned on that smaller base. The mistake is treating the whole check as income. Then two mirror-image risks. Prepayment risk: rates fall, homeowners refinance, principal comes back early, and you reinvest lower with little price gain, because of that embedded call. Extension risk: rates rise, homeowners stay put, principal comes back late, and the average life gets longer. Simple tell: early cash is prepayment, late cash is extension. The exam trap: only GNMA and Farm Credit carry the direct guarantee; Fannie, Freddie and Sallie are indirect. To a client: these pay you monthly, but part of every check is your own money coming back, and if rates drop, people refinance and you get more of it back early, just when reinvesting pays less.

debt.at: Municipal bonds and taxable equivalent yield
debt.say: Municipal bonds. Muni interest is generally exempt from regular federal income tax, and usually state-tax free only for residents of the issuing state. The types rank by risk. General obligation bonds are backed by taxing power, full faith and credit, and are the lowest risk. Revenue bonds are repaid from the income of the financed facility, like an airport, so they're riskier and yield more. Private activity bonds carry the most credit risk, and nonexempt ones are federally taxable. Insured munis lower credit risk and let the issuer cut the coupon. Now the formula you'll use constantly: taxable equivalent yield equals the tax-exempt yield divided by one minus the marginal rate. Going the other way, a taxable bond's after-tax yield is its yield times one minus the rate. Walk it at a twenty-four percent bracket. The muni yields three point three percent; divided by point seven six, that's about four point three four percent. The corporate yields five percent; times point seven six, three point eight after tax. Either way the corporate wins. Bump the bracket to thirty-five percent and the muni's equivalent becomes about five point oh eight, so now the muni wins. The classic error is multiplying the muni yield by one minus t instead of dividing. And the exam trap when state tax shows up: tax each bond only where it's taxable. Treasuries, federal only. In-state munis, neither. Out-of-state munis, state only. Corporates, both. To a client: a three point three percent tax-free bond is like earning about four point three percent taxable in your bracket, and the higher your bracket, the better munis look.

Corporates, zeros and foreign bonds. Most corporates are debentures, unsecured; subordinated debentures pay more but still rank ahead of common stock. Callable corporates are less attractive, with call protection generally at least ten years. Zero-coupon bonds are deep-discount OID bonds: no reinvestment risk, the most price-volatile, and taxable zeros create phantom income, so they belong in tax-deferred accounts. Now a tax distinction the exam loves: OID versus market discount. OID means the bond was issued below par, and it's taxed yearly as it accrues. Market discount means the value fell after issue, and it's generally taxed at sale or maturity, as interest up to the accrued discount. Walk it: a par-issued bond bought at nine forty and sold at nine ninety, with thirty-five dollars of accrued market discount. Total gain is fifty dollars; thirty-five is interest income and only fifteen is capital gain. Calling all fifty a capital gain is the mistake. Foreign bonds next. A Yankee bond is in dollars, sold in the U.S., so no currency risk for a U.S. buyer. A Eurodollar bond is dollars sold outside the U.S., not SEC registered. A Eurobond is in any currency not native to where it's issued, and usually carries currency risk. Bulldogs and samurais are pounds and yen. The trap: Eurobond does not mean euros, and Yankee bonds remove currency risk. To a client: a zero is like a savings bond for a specific date, bought cheap and paying the full amount when your daughter starts college, with no checks along the way and the growth still taxed yearly, so it belongs in a tax-sheltered account.

Convertible bond math: five numbers, and the denominators are the whole game. A convertible is a straight bond plus an option to swap into a fixed number of the issuer's shares. The setup: one-thousand-dollar par, four percent semiannual coupon, ten years left, straight bonds yielding six percent, a conversion price of sixty-two fifty, the stock at fifty-five, and the convertible trading at a thousand. Conversion ratio is par over conversion price, so a thousand over sixty-two fifty, sixteen shares. Conversion value is the ratio times the stock price, not the conversion price: sixteen times fifty-five, eight hundred eighty dollars. Investment value is the bond priced as a plain bond at the straight rate: twenty periods, three percent, twenty-dollar payments, thousand-dollar face, which gives eight hundred fifty-one twenty-three. The floor is the greater of the two, eight eighty. Conversion premium is price minus conversion value, a hundred twenty dollars, divided by conversion value: thirteen point six four percent. Investment premium is price minus investment value, one forty-eight seventy-seven, divided by investment value: seventeen point four eight percent. Downside risk is those same dollars divided by today's price: fourteen point eight eight percent. That's the trap. Investment premium and downside risk share the same dollars but use different denominators. Premium over X divides by X; how far could it fall divides by today's price. To a client: you're paying about seventeen percent more than this is worth as a plain bond for a chance at the stock's upside, and if the stock tanks, the bond value is the cushion, roughly a fifteen percent drop from today, though that shifts if rates move.

Portfolio structures. Immunization sets interest rate risk against reinvestment risk. When rates rise, prices fall but coupons reinvest higher; when rates fall, the reverse. They fully offset when portfolio duration equals the liability's duration, the time horizon. Pensions, endowments and insurers use it most; individuals use it for goals like tuition. A zero-coupon bond's duration equals its maturity, so one zero maturing on the goal date immunizes it. A coupon bond's duration is shorter than its maturity, so pick a maturity somewhat beyond the horizon. And it isn't fully passive, because portfolio duration falls faster than liability duration, so you rebalance. Quick check: seven-year horizon, a seven-year zero or a seven-year six percent coupon bond? The zero. Now the three shapes. A ladder puts equal amounts at staggered maturities, say a hundred fifty thousand split into thirty thousand at one through five years, and each year the maturing rung buys a new five-year bond. It's passive and yields more than an all-short portfolio. A barbell holds only short and long bonds, and it's the active one: the long end locks rates, the short end frees cash. A bullet is bought over time so everything matures on one date. For ninety thousand needed in eight years, buy an eight-year bond now, a six-year in year two, a four-year in year four. The traps: short plus long only is a barbell, not a ladder; and with coupon bonds, match duration, not maturity, to the horizon. To a client: we'll stagger your bonds so one matures every year. If rates rise, the money coming due gets reinvested higher; if they fall, the longer bonds have already locked in today's rate.

Bond swaps: selling one bond and buying another to raise yield, save taxes, or cut interest rate risk. There are five, and the exam tests them by motive. A substitution swap moves into an identical bond priced differently, a short-lived arbitrage. An intermarket spread swap moves between sectors, like governments and corporates, when one looks mispriced against the other. A rate anticipation swap is built on a forecast: go from long to short if you expect rates to rise, short to long if you expect them to fall. A pure yield pickup swap moves from a lower-yielding bond to a higher-yielding one, longer or lower quality, with no forecast at all. And a tax swap sells a bond at a loss and reinvests the proceeds, to capture the tax saving from the capital loss. Walk the tax swap. A client paid twenty thousand dollars for bonds now worth eighteen thousand because rates rose, and the marginal rate is twenty-four percent. The loss is two thousand dollars, and the textbook's simplified saving is two thousand times point two four, four hundred eighty dollars. The eighteen thousand gets reinvested and held to maturity. Two mistakes to avoid: calling the whole two thousand the saving, or applying the tax rate to the proceeds instead of the loss. The exam trap: pure yield pickup has no rate forecast; rate anticipation does. If the question mentions an expectation about rates, think rate anticipation. To a client: this bond is down only because rates rose, so we can sell it, book the loss to cut your tax bill, and buy a similar bond so your income keeps coming.

debt.at: Matching fixed income to the investor
debt.say: Matching fixed income to the investor. Always start with the goal: stability of principal and income, or capital gains. Stability seekers fit T-bills, money market funds, funds holding triple-A issues, and low-duration bonds. Capital-gain seekers fit zero-coupon bonds, high-yield bond funds, and long-duration funds. Price sensitivity rises with lower coupons, longer maturities and lower yields. So if you expect rates to fall, go long maturity and low coupon, which is high duration; if you expect them to rise, go short maturity and high coupon, low duration. Now the textbook's client pairings. High bracket: munis, after computing the taxable equivalent yield. Taxable buyer worried about default in a high-tax state: Treasuries. Wants more yield than Treasuries: agencies, but check call protection. Needs a set sum on a set date: Treasury zeros maturing then. Retiree wanting inflation-adjusted yearly cash: a TIPS ladder in a traditional IRA. Wants income plus upside: convertibles. Wants diversification: foreign bonds, Yankees to avoid currency risk. Walk the example: a client needs fifty thousand dollars in seven years, in a taxable account. Buy seven-year Treasury zeros with fifty thousand of face value: no default risk, known payoff. The accrued interest is taxed yearly, so pay it from other funds. A bond fund has no fixed maturity and coupon bonds carry reinvestment risk, so neither fits a fixed-date goal. The exam trap: aggressive investors go long duration only when they expect rates to fall. To a client: retiring doesn't mean your money's job is short-term, since you could need it for twenty-five years, so we'll stagger maturities and protect against inflation instead of parking it all in T-bills.

Yield curves. A yield curve plots yield against maturity for bonds of the same quality, and the Treasury curve is the most watched because its shape shifts with the economic cycle. Normal, or positive, means long rates above short, signaling expansion with rates expected to rise. Flat suggests the economy is peaking, with little rate change expected. Inverted means short rates above long: the Fed tightened against inflation, rates are expected to fall, and a recession is possible. Now the three theories. Unbiased expectations says the long rate is the geometric mean of today's short rate and the expected future short rates, and it can explain any shape. Liquidity preference says investors need a premium to lend long, so it explains only an upward curve. Market segmentation says supply and demand within maturity segments set rates as institutions match their liabilities. Walk the math. The one-year rate is two and a half percent, and next year's one-year rate is expected at three and a half. Multiply one point oh two five by one point oh three five to get about one point oh six oh nine, take the square root, about one point oh three, so the two-year rate is about three percent. Expected higher short rates produce an upward curve. The mistakes are skipping the root, which gives six point oh nine. The exam trap: only liquidity preference is limited to an upward slope. To a client: normally you get paid more to lend longer, and when short bonds pay more than long ones, the market expects rates to come down, which has sometimes come before a recession.

debt.at: Using yield curves to make decisions
debt.say: Using yield curves to make decisions, and this one's counterintuitive, so slow down. With a flat curve, you get no pay for extending past the flat point, so buy long only if you're highly confident rates will fall soon. The risks are that long rates rise to restore a premium, or the whole curve shifts up. With an inverted curve, the Fed has raised short rates to fight inflation, and the textbook's answer is to buy long, call-protected bonds. Why? When the curve normalizes, short rates fall the most and long bonds gain the most. With a steep curve in the early years, income investors can extend a little for a big yield pickup. But if the curve is steep because of inflation fears, avoid long-term bonds. Walk the inverted example. One-year bills yield five point two percent, twenty-year call-protected bonds yield four point four, and the client expects the curve to normalize. The bills pay more today, but they mature in a year and get reinvested at lower rates. The twenty-year bond locks in four point four percent for two decades and rises in price as rates fall. Call protection matters because it keeps the issuer from refinancing your bond away right when rates drop. The common mistakes are chasing the higher short yield, or buying long bonds that can be called soon. The exam trap, said plainly: with an inverted curve, the answer is long-term bonds, not the higher-yielding short end. To a client: short-term rates look great today, but they won't last, so locking in a long, non-callable bond now keeps your income high after rates drop, and the bond's price should rise too.

Last piece of this tab: preferred stock, a hybrid. It pays a fixed dividend set as a percentage of par, but the board has to declare it. It's paid before common dividends and has no maturity, it's a perpetuity, so its price moves inversely with rates, and more than the same firm's bonds. Cumulative preferred means skipped dividends, called arrears, must be paid before any common dividend. Corporate holders get a dividends-received deduction: fifty percent if they own less than twenty percent, sixty-five percent if they own twenty percent or more, within limits. How is it like a bond? Fixed cash flow, no vote, callable, may have sinking funds, and ahead of common in bankruptcy. How is it unlike one? The issuer can't deduct the dividends, a missed dividend isn't bankruptcy, and it pays quarterly instead of semiannually. The valuation is simple: value equals the annual dividend divided by the required return. Walk it: a hundred-dollar par, four and a half percent preferred pays four fifty a year. If market yields rise to six percent, four fifty divided by point oh six is seventy-five dollars, down twenty-five percent. If yields fall to four percent, it's a hundred twelve fifty, up twelve and a half percent. Notice the price doesn't stay at par just because the dividend is fixed. The exam trap: the dividend is a percent of par, not market price, and preferred pays quarterly. To a client: preferreds pay a steady dividend ahead of common shareholders, but they never mature, so if rates rise their price can drop more than a bond's. They fit best when rates look steady or falling.
